description:
SIMER (Simer Interplanetary Mars EVA Routing)

We’re Khalifa University engineering students who build and ship AI products, with tons of hackathon wins behind us. Our skills: machine learning and computer vision, generative models, iOS and web apps, AWS cloud and UI/UX. We want to turn Mars data into something that simmers in people's minds.
summary:
SIMER (Simer Interplanetary Mars EVA Routing) is a decision-support system for planning astronaut surface traverses (EVAs) at Jezero Crater, Mars, built entirely on public NASA, USGS and ESA data. It combines orbital imagery, a 20 m terrain model, the USGS geologic map, and Perseverance’s traverse and sample sites in one layered map.

For any set of scientific targets, SIMER generates four candidate routes: balanced, fastest, safest and maximum science. It tests each route against the constraints that govern crew safety: oxygen reserve, the margin to return at every step, slope, terrain trafficability, radio line of sight to the habitat, and daylight. Each route gets a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict, with every finding quantified and its source labelled. Crews can rehearse the traverse in 3D or low-cost VR, navigate with live hazard alerts, and re-plan in natural language through an AI copilot that is limited to the planner’s own outputs.

One-way radio signals between Earth and Mars take up to 22 minutes, so Mars crews will have to make EVA decisions on their own. SIMER gives them a planner they can check, question and trust.
details:
Overview

When the first crews walk on Mars, a question to Mission Control can take up to 44 minutes to answer, so every decision on a Marswalk will be made by the crew on the spot. SIMER (Simer Interplanetary Mars EVA Routing) is a decision-support system that helps them make those decisions . It layers data from six NASA missions and ESA’s Mars Express, together with USGS terrain and geologic maps, into a single map. For any set of science stops, SIMER plans four routes (balanced, fastest, safest and max science) on a 20 m terrain model. It checks each route against explicit safety rules and gives a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict, with the number behind every finding. One plan runs on three displays (habitat, tablet and helmet visor) with live hazard alerts. Crews can rehearse the walk in VR, and an AI copilot answers their questions using only the planner’s outputs. Because Mars has no satellite navigation, SIMER also contributes SIMER-Loc, a self-supervised network that locates the crew by matching ground views to HiRISE orbital imagery. In simulation, it fixes position to within 1 m in 96% of hard trials, against 83% for a JPL-style census baseline.


1. What SIMER does and how it works

Every EVA runs through three steps:

  • Plan: choose the stops and get four routes.
  • Check: each route gets a verdict, with its reasons.
  • Walk: follow the route with turn-by-turn guidance.

1.1 Data foundation

A Python pipeline (rasterio, pyogrio, shapely, NumPy) crops the USGS Mars 2020 CTX digital terrain model (20 m/px) and orthomosaic (6 m/px) to the Jezero site. It rasterises the USGS SIM 3464 geologic units onto the same 20 m grid. It attaches Perseverance’s traverse and waypoints (NASA/JPL MMGIS), the Mars 2020 sample list (name, rock type and sol sealed) and the Three Forks sample depot.

NASA Mars Trek supplies six base layers:

  • HiRISE (25 cm)
  • CTX
  • THEMIS day IR
  • THEMIS night IR, where loose sand and dust read cold and rock reads warm (Edwards et al. 2011)
  • MOLA blended with HRSC from ESA’s Mars Express
  • Viking colour

Mars Trek also supplies Mastcam-Z 360° panoramas, so the crew can see a stop before walking to it. It also supplies the outline of NASA Exploration Zone 1034, the Jezero region proposed for human missions at NASA’s first landing-site workshop.

A conditions panel brings together:

  • the season and sun times from Mars24
  • the dust-storm season: regional storms cluster at Ls 180–340° (Kass et al. 2016)
  • the hours when dust devils are most likely, from Perseverance’s weather station, MEDA (Newman et al. 2022)
  • the Curiosity RAD surface dose rate of 0.64 mSv/day for an EVA dose estimate (Hassler et al. 2014)
  • the Earth–Mars light time from JPL planetary positions (Standish 1992)

Analysis layers derived from the terrain cover walking hazard, slope, geology, science value, radio coverage and a survival envelope (the oxygen needed to return from any point).

1.2 Route planning

The planner runs on the crew’s own device.

  • It computes slope with Horn’s method and walking speed with Tobler’s hiking function.
  • It computes metabolic rate with the Pandolf load-carriage model scaled to Mars gravity (astronaut 80 kg, suit and life support 60 kg, suit effort factor ×1.4). Oxygen use follows from the metabolic rate.
  • Routes come from an A* search over a 16-connected grid, refined by any-angle smoothing.
  • Ground steeper than the no-go slope (25°) is removed from the search, so no route can cross it.
  • A Dijkstra field gives the oxygen needed to return home from every cell.

Every cell carries two scores derived from the data:

  • Walking hazard combines slope (rising from 5° to the no-go limit), roughness from the terrain model, and wind-blown sand from the geologic map.
  • Science value comes from the SIM 3464 geologic units. Each unit has a weight set by the team, with the delta and crater-rim units highest. Cells within 40 m of a contact between two units get a +0.15 bonus, because contacts show how units relate. Wind-blown sand gets no bonus.

The four profiles differ only in what they charge per second of walking:

  • Fastest: walking time.
  • Safest: time × (1 + 4 × hazard), plus 30% wherever the habitat radio is out of sight.
  • Max science: time × (1 − 0.6 × science value, never below 0.4) × (1 + 0.5 × hazard). High-value ground costs up to 60% less, so the route bends toward the delta and unit contacts when the extra walking is affordable.
  • Balanced: time × (1 + 1.5 × hazard) × (1 − 0.3 × science value, never below 0.7), plus 10% out of radio sight.

Every route reports a science score from 0 to 100: the mean science value along the path. The reference EVA scores 65. When the most direct line already crosses high-value ground, Max science and Fastest converge.

Figure 1. The planning view. The crew sets scientific targets (here the Three Forks Sample Depot and Swift Run) and SIMER draws the candidate routes over HiRISE imagery, with the walking-hazard layer shown. The panel gives start time, local sunset, dust conditions and the verdict for the selected route.

1.3 Explainable verdicts

Written rules give each route a GO, CAUTION or NO-GO verdict, and each reason is stated with its number. Every threshold is an editable planning assumption, not a NASA requirement. The defaults are below.

NO-GO

  • Oxygen reserve: the walk must end with at least 15% of the 600 L of usable suit O₂.
  • Suit time: the EVA must not exceed 7 h.
  • Daylight: the crew must be home before the sun drops below 5°. Sun position comes from the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm.
  • Slope: ground above 25° is excluded from every route.

CAUTION

  • Walk-back margin: at every step, the O₂ left must be at least ×1.25 the O₂ needed to walk home.
  • Slope: any stretch steeper than 15°.
  • Radio: any loss of line of sight to the habitat’s 10 m mast, meaning a relay is needed. Suit radio range is 8 km.

Flagged along the route: loose sand, dust-devil hours (11:00–14:00 local solar time) and hazards reported by the crew.

Every value in the interface is labelled DATA, DERIVED, MODEL, ASSUMPTION or SIMULATED, and every assumption can be edited and re-run. On the reference EVA, four checks pass, one is CAUTION (radio) and none is NO-GO.

Figure 2. The reference EVA as recorded in the mission brief, drawn on the MRO CTX orthomosaic. Numbers mark the stops in visiting order; the square marks the notional habitat.

1.4 Execution on three displays

The habitat display hands the plan to the crew's tablet with a QR code or link. Only the definition of the plan is sent (start, targets, time, route profile and changed assumptions). The tablet recomputes identical routes and verdicts on its own copy of the terrain. During the walk, SIMER gives turn-by-turn guidance, an oxygen gauge, time to return, sun elevation and the latest position fix. The guidance appears on the habitat display, on the crew tablet and in the helmet visor.

Figure 3. One walk, three screens: the habitat display (centre), the crew tablet (right) and the stereo helmet HUD (lower left), all showing the same plan and the next manoeuvre.

1.5 Radio awareness and hazard response

SIMER computes line of sight from the habitat's radio mast across the CTX terrain model with the XDraw viewshed algorithm, and warns the crew before each dead zone. For other hazards, such as a dust storm, a single “Head home now” action re-plans the fastest safe return from the crew's current position. Crews can report new hazards, which are then flagged to everyone on the route. Storm events are clearly labelled SIMULATED, because no live dust-storm feed from Mars exists.

Figure 4. (a) Radio dead-zone warning on the crew tablet, 310 m before the crew loses line of sight to the habitat for about an hour (mast 10 m); the warning is labelled DERIVED. (b) A simulated dust-storm warning, with the options to head home or keep going.

1.6 Rehearsal and records

Crews can rehearse the walk in VR before stepping outside. The terrain is real and is lit by the Mars sun for the planned time of day, from a phone in Google Cardboard to a WebXR headset. An AI copilot turns natural-language requests into planner calls and quotes only the planner's numbers. A rule-based copilot takes over when there is no network. Other features cover the whole EVA: a printable mission brief, a sol planner that packs sample sites into one EVA per sol, a field log, voice alerts, and a post-EVA report that compares the plan with the walk.

Figure 5. The helmet visor in VR rehearsal, drawn for each eye of a Google Cardboard viewer. The route ribbon runs at the walker’s feet. The display keeps to the edges: compass heading, suit O₂, radio status, sun elevation, time on the walk, and the next turn (2.4 km, bear right to Three Forks).

1.7 Self-location without GPS: SIMER-Loc

Mars has no satellite navigation, so a crew must find its own position before it can follow a route. Rovers do this by matching their own images to orbital maps. SIMER-Loc applies the same idea to a helmet camera.

Method. SIMER-Loc assumes a stereo helmet camera, like Perseverance’s Navcam.

  • Stereo depth projects each view through its camera model into a top-down ground map: 0.3 m/px, visible to about 30 m, heading unknown.
  • That map and a HiRISE window around the prior position (25 cm resampled to 0.3 m/px, prior ± 40 m) pass through the same descriptor function.
  • An FFT correlation then scores every position for all 120 candidate headings at once.
  • A coarse search at 1.2 m/px keeps the two best places. A fine search at 0.3 m/px refines them over ±4° in 0.5° steps, with a sub-pixel peak fit.
  • A fix (east, north, heading) is accepted only if it is unique, judged by the ratio of the second-best match to the best.

The search follows the JPL-style method; only the per-pixel descriptor is new. A 67,120-parameter convolutional network (a 273 KB checkpoint) replaces the 25-bit census signature with 16 unit-length channels per pixel. One network runs at three scales: 0.3, 1.2 and 5 m/px.

Figure 6. The SIMER-Loc pipeline. The ground view and the orbital map pass through the same descriptor f(·) (blue), the only learned component. The correlation and search follow the JPL-style method unchanged. The dashed path is used only in training: a softmax over the whole correlation surface, with cross-entropy at the true position.Figure 7. What the network learns: (a) a HiRISE orbital patch; (b) its 16-channel descriptors, shown as RGB through the first three principal components; (c) the same ground seen from orbit and from a simulated rover receives matching descriptors.

Training. Training is self-supervised on NASA imagery only. The true match is known by construction, so no hand labels are needed.

  • The network saw 21,120 pairs (660 steps over 12 epochs, about 9 minutes on an Apple M4 GPU, seed 2026).
  • Pairs combine simulated rover maps with HiRISE at 1.2 and 0.3 m/px, and real CTX with HiRISE at 5 m/px.
  • Every training pixel lies at least 1 km from the rover route, and every test site lies on it, so test ground is never seen in training.

Validation used 24 trials with 12 m of visible ground, harsh light and a prior up to 50 m off. The JPL-style search with an untrained descriptor already fixes 75% of positions within 1 m. Training lifts this to 88% by epoch 9, against 42% for our earlier v1 network and 33% for census.
Figure 8. Training of SIMER-Loc Net v2: loss, validation self-location, median position error and top-1 match rate by scale, with the census and NCC baselines on the same trials.

Figure 9. Self-location in simulation: (a) the rover's top-down view; (b) the match on the HiRISE map; (c) the fixed track along the walk.

Evaluation. Test sites were fixed before evaluation, and every trial runs all three methods on the same rover map and prior.

  • The simulated rover views sit at real Perseverance positions under hard conditions: harsh light, 50 m prior error, 60 m search.
  • A second test uses only real data: 238 CTX patches, from a different camera, located on the HiRISE map.

Results:

  • Across 432 hard trials, SIMER-Loc beats census 74 to 2 on the trials where the two disagree (exact McNemar p = 7.7 × 10⁻²⁰).
  • When every method succeeds, all three are accurate to within centimetres (medians 1.6–7.2 cm), far inside the 1 m a walker needs.
  • SIMER-Loc locates all 238 real CTX patches on the HiRISE map, more than either baseline.
  • On a simulated 2.4 km walk with a fix every 300 m, the position is never more than 13 m off, against 20 m with dead reckoning alone.


Figure 10. Hard benchmark: fixes within 1 m against how much ground the rover sees (harsh light, 50 m prior error, 60 m search; 72 trials per point, 95% confidence intervals).

1.8 Verification

  • Automated tests (Vitest) check the sun model against the published Mars24 worked example, and check that A* returns optimal paths on the real Jezero terrain.
    • Cutting usable suit O₂ from 600 L to 175 L turns the reference EVA NO-GO: it ends with 23 L against a 26 L reserve.
    • Lowering the suit-time limit to 2 h makes the 2 h 37 min EVA NO-GO.
    • A late start fails the daylight rule.
  • The outputs agree with each other. The 70 µSv EVA dose is the RAD rate (0.64 mSv/day) applied over the 2 h 37 min EVA. Oxygen use of 152 L, about 1 L/min, follows from the Pandolf rate.
  • All four routes are planned in about a second in a browser.

2. Benefits

  • Traceability. Every figure shown to the crew carries its origin (data, derived, model, assumption or simulated), and every assumption can be edited and re-run.
  • Safety by construction. The margin to return to the habitat is checked at every step of the route, not only at the turnaround point.
  • Early warning. Radio dead zones, steep slopes, loose sand and storms are flagged before the crew reaches them, with a one-action route home.
  • Bounded AI. Routes, verdicts and figures come from deterministic planning code. The language-model copilot only reports those outputs, and a rule-based copilot keeps the system working offline.
  • Low-cost access. The system runs in a browser, and immersive rehearsal needs only a smartphone and a Cardboard viewer.
  • A measured path to GPS-free navigation. SIMER-Loc is benchmarked against established baselines on identical trials.

3. Intended impact

One-way radio signals between Earth and Mars take 3 to 22 minutes, so an answer from mission control can take up to 44 minutes. Crews will have to decide on the spot whether to continue, re-route or return. SIMER shows how an onboard planner can support those decisions with reasoning the crew can verify, question and trust. The same approach can serve human-mission concept studies, Mars analogue field campaigns, and teaching with real planetary data. SIMER-Loc's benchmark gives a clear starting point for camera-based crew localisation.

4. Tools, languages, hardware and software

5. Creativity

SIMER brings the plan, check, navigate and re-plan cycle of everyday navigation apps to planetary exploration. It uses that cycle to combine orbital science data, human physiology, radio propagation and celestial mechanics in one browser application. One plan drives three displays, from the habitat to the helmet visor, and crews can physically walk a route in VR before committing to it. SIMER-Loc keeps the proven JPL-style localisation search and replaces only its hand-designed census signature with a learned one. Because that signature is trained without labels on NASA imagery alone, it can be tested directly against the method it replaces.

6. Factors the team considered

  • Crew safety: oxygen reserve, return margin, suit endurance, daylight, slope, terrain trafficability and dust activity.
  • Operational autonomy: the communication delay between Earth and Mars sets the design.
  • Trust in AI: the language model is limited to verified planner outputs, with a deterministic fallback.
  • Scientific integrity: every source is cited, every figure is labelled by type, and simulated events are marked as such.
  • Experimental rigour: all localisation methods run on identical trials, test sites were fixed before evaluation, and training ground is at least 1 km from every test site.
